claims.text: Decreasing nanoparticle or grain size increases grain-boundary density.
At high temperature, higher grain-boundary density provides accelerated atomic-diffusion pathways.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion promotes chemical segregation.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion promotes phase transformation and phase degradation.
Higher grain-boundary density promotes oxidation under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Diffusion-driven segregation and degradation in small nanoalloys overwhelm stabilization from configurational entropy.
The starting nanoalloys are well mixed, chemically homogeneous, and structurally uniform at the nanometer scale.
The controlled comparison varies nanoparticle or grain size while holding alloy composition and processing conditions constant.
Larger grains have fewer grain boundaries than smaller grains.
Larger-grained nanoalloys maintain structural homogeneity primarily because of configurational-entropy stabilization.
After identical high-temperature exposure, small-grain samples will exhibit more chemical segregation than large-grain samples.
After identical high-temperature exposure, small-grain samples will exhibit more phase degradation than large-grain samples.
After identical high-temperature exposure, small-grain samples will exhibit more oxidation than large-grain samples.
Small-grain samples will retain a less stable microstructure and a more altered phase composition than the large-grain baseline.
The prediction is restricted to exposure temperatures of 800–1000°C and durations sufficient to activate grain-boundary diffusion.
Significantly lower temperatures may not produce the predicted size-dependent degradation.
Inert atmospheres may not produce the same size-dependent behavior as oxidizing atmospheres.
The size threshold and degradation kinetics may depend on alloy composition.
Failure of the small-grain samples to show significantly greater segregation, phase degradation, or oxidation than the large-grain controls would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
